sections.skill: Describe parameters as learned settings that capture patterns

questions.prompt: What are parameters in a model?

choices.text: The questions users type into the finished app
The list of every training example, kept word for word
The rules a programmer wrote out line by line
The adjustable numbers set during training

questions.correct_answer: The adjustable numbers set during training
questions.intro: During training, a model adjusts a huge set of numbers called PARAMETERS (sometimes called weights). You can picture them as millions or billions of tiny dials. Each time the model's output is wrong on a training example, the dials are nudged a little so that next time the output is closer. After enough nudges, the dial settings capture PATTERNS in the data, for example which pixel shapes usually mean "cat." The model keeps the dial settings, not a neat copy of every example, although it can sometimes reproduce pieces of text or images it saw many times. More parameters can capture more patterns, but size alone does not guarantee better results.
questions.feedback: Parameters are numbers the training process adjusts.

sections.skill: Picture tuning a guitar by ear

questions.prompt: In the comparison, what are the guitar pegs like?

choices.text: The model's parameters
The app's screen
The training examples
The user's questions

questions.correct_answer: The model's parameters
questions.intro: Imagine tuning a guitar by ear. You pluck a string, hear that it is a little flat, and turn the peg slightly. You pluck again and turn again, until it sounds right. You do not write down every sound you heard; what you keep is the final peg position. A model's PARAMETERS are like millions of pegs. Training plucks, listens and turns: each wrong output nudges the pegs a little. What the model keeps afterward is the peg settings, which capture what "sounding right" means for its task.
questions.feedback: Pegs are adjustable settings, like parameters.

questions.prompt: What do you do when a string sounds flat?

choices.text: Stop playing for good

Write down the sound and keep it forever
Turn the peg a little and try again

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Avoid oversimplified claims about what a model stores

questions.prompt: A user asks a company to "delete the fact about me from the model." Why is this hard?

choices.text: Learned patterns are spread across settings, not stored as one fact
Models store each fact in a labeled folder that is locked
It is easy; any user can delete one parameter
Models never learn anything about people

questions.correct_answer: Learned patterns are spread across settings, not stored as one fact
questions.intro: Because learned patterns are stored as dial settings rather than as a list of facts, you usually cannot open a model and look up "the" fact it learned or delete one example's influence by hand. This is one reason models can mix patterns in surprising ways: an answer may blend several sources into something no single source said. It also explains why models sometimes reproduce memorized passages: text repeated very often in training can leave strong traces. Claims such as "the model just copies" or "the model never copies" are both too simple.
questions.feedback: Influence is spread across many parameters.

questions.prompt: A model's answer blends ideas so that no single source said exactly that. What explains this?

choices.text: It always copies one source exactly

It has a written rule never to use any real sources
It combines learned patterns from many examples

questions.correct_answer: It combines learned patterns from many examples
